sections.h2: How do I get a deed recorded in Oscoda County?
sections.html:
Oscoda County combines the Clerk and the Register of Deeds in one office at 311 South Morenci Avenue in Mio, MI 48647, inside the Government Administration Building downtown. The mailing address is PO Box 399, Mio, MI 48647. The phone is 989-826-1110, the fax is 989-826-1136, and the email is countyclerk@oscodacountymi.com.

The office is open Monday to Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., closed for lunch from noon to 1 p.m., and closed on most federal holidays. No appointment is needed. A deed can reach the office three ways:

  • Hand delivery at the Mio counter.
  • Regular USPS mail to the PO Box, ideally with a self-addressed stamped envelope for the return of the original.
  • UPS or FedEx delivery to the street address.

Out-of-area title agents can also use electronic recording through CSC Ingeo, EPN (E-Recording Partners) or Simplifile. The office warns that certified court documents and death certificates cannot go through e-recording, so call before you try to send those.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a deed in Oscoda County?
sections.html:
The county's Register of Deeds page does not print a fee list, so the amounts below come from the state fee statute, MCL 600.2567, which covers Oscoda County. Call 989-826-1110 to confirm the total, including any card or e-recording vendor surcharge, before you mail a check.

Michigan register of deeds fees under MCL 600.2567(1), on the Michigan Legislature site
ItemState fee
Entering and recording a document, any page count$30.00
Each added instrument assigned or discharged by one document$3.00
Copies of records$1.00 per page
Certifying a recorded document$5.00
Grantor/grantee search by staff50 cents per year searched, minimum $5.00
Filing any other paper$1.00

Of each $30, the statute directs $5 into the county's automation fund. The statute counts a page as one side of a sheet no smaller than 8.5 by 11 inches and no larger than 8.5 by 14. Copies must be taken as paper, and the office does not allow photos of records.

sections.h2: How is transfer tax figured on an Oscoda County sale?
sections.html:
Michigan charges two real estate transfer taxes on a deed, and both use the sale price in blocks of $500. The state rate is $3.75 per block under MCL 207.525. The county rate is 55 cents per block under MCL 207.504, because Oscoda County has far fewer than 2,000,000 residents. The deed must state the full value, or an affidavit of value goes with it.

Take a $125,000 sale, close to Oscoda County's median owner-occupied home value of $125,500. That is 250 blocks. The state tax is $937.50, the county tax is $137.50, and the pair comes to $1,075. A partial block counts as a whole one, so a price of $125,100 adds a block.

Several transfers pay nothing, and the two statutes do not match line for line:

  • A deed with consideration under $100 is exempt from both taxes.
  • A transfer ordered by a court of record, with no price set by the court, is exempt from both.
  • A boundary-line fix with no money changing hands is exempt from both.
  • A deed given only to confirm a title already vested, such as a quitclaim that corrects a flaw, is exempt from both.
  • A conveyance from a parent to a child or grandchild is exempt from the state tax only.

Write the exemption on the face of the deed.

sections.h2: What records and protections does the Oscoda County office keep?
sections.html:
The office holds real estate records back to the late 1800s. Land records from 1985 to the present are stored electronically, and anything older is searchable on microfiche. Documents appear online within five days of recording. Every new filing is time and date stamped, checked for the recording requirements, given a document number, indexed and scanned.

Searches run by property owner's name. The office has several public computer terminals, but it does not perform title searches, so it points people to a title company or private searcher. Ownership is established by what the recorded documents say, which means a seller with an old, unrecorded deed in a drawer should record it before listing.

Online access comes in three forms. Fidlar Laredo is a subscription tool with a software download, built for heavy users. Fidlar Tapestry is pay-as-you-go and covers several Michigan counties. A free direct search is also available through the county's Fidlar link.

Property Fraud Alert is free to Oscoda County owners and can be started at 1-800-728-3858 or at propertyfraudalert.com/mioscoda. It notifies you in real time when a document is recorded against your property. The county page notes that Michigan's Youngblood Law, House Bills 5598 and 5599, signed in November 2024, makes it a felony to submit a fraudulent document to any Michigan register of deeds.

sections.h2: What documents and certificates does a deed need in Oscoda County?
sections.html:
The register does not prepare documents or supply legal forms, and the county suggests an attorney or title company for drafting. For a do-it-yourself seller it lists MichiganLegalHelp.org and eforms.com as places to start. The office also does not give legal advice about how a deed should be prepared.

MCL 565.201 sets what the register may accept. The signer's name must be printed under the signature in black or dark blue ink, and the grantee's address and the drafter's name and address must appear. After April 1, 1997 the first page needs a 2.5 inch blank top margin, and a statement of the recordable event on the first line.

Tax proof is a separate step. MCL 211.135 asks for a county treasurer's certificate that no tax liens or titles are held against the parcel and that the preceding five years of taxes are paid. A quitclaim or other conveyance with no covenant of warranty is excused. Ask the Oscoda County Treasurer for the certificate when you plan a warranty deed, and bring it with the deed to the Mio office.

sections.h2: What is selling a house in Oscoda County like?
sections.html:
Oscoda County is the only Michigan county with no incorporated city or village. Mio, the county seat, is a census-designated place in the Au Sable River valley, and M-33 and M-72 meet there. The southern half of the county lies inside the Huron National Forest, and much of the land sits on the Grayling outwash plain of sand ridges, jack pine and hardwoods. The county was created in 1840 and organized in 1881.

The 2020 census counted 8,219 residents, the fewest in any Lower Peninsula county, and the Census Bureau estimates 8,723 for July 2025. For 2020 to 2024 the median owner-occupied home value was $125,500, with 87.2% of homes owner-occupied and 32.8% of residents aged 65 or older. Median household income was $49,515 and median gross rent was $681. The county has 7,792 housing units but only 3,788 households, so many houses are seasonal or vacant, and the Bureau recorded 24 building permits for 2025.

Before you list a cabin or woodland house, search the owner's name at the register and ask the county treasurer for the tax certificate. Both steps affect how fast a closing can happen.

faqs.q: Where is the Oscoda County Register of Deeds located?
faqs.a: It is at 311 South Morenci Avenue in Mio, MI 48647, in the Government Administration Building. Mail goes to PO Box 399, and the phone is 989-826-1110.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed in Oscoda County by mail?
faqs.a: Yes. Send the original to Register of Deeds, PO Box 399, Mio, MI 48647, or ship by UPS or FedEx to the street address. The office likes a self-addressed stamped envelope so the recorded original comes back to you.

faqs.q: Does Oscoda County accept electronic recording of deeds?
faqs.a: Yes, through CSC Ingeo, EPN and Simplifile. Certified court documents and death certificates are not accepted that way, so call the office to learn whether a particular document can be e-recorded.

faqs.q: How much transfer tax will I owe on a $100,000 Oscoda County sale?
faqs.a: You owe $860 if no exemption applies. The state tax is $750 at $3.75 per $500, and the county tax is $110 at 55 cents per $500.

faqs.q: Does the Oscoda County register search titles for sellers?
faqs.a: No. The office is a recording office, and it tells people to use a title company or private searcher. You can search by owner name yourself at the public terminals or online.
